companies.name: Arup
companies.tagline: Trust-owned global engineering, design and advisory consultancy working across 150+ disciplines in the built environment.

facts.v: 1946 in London by engineer Ove Arup (as Ove N. Arup Consulting Engineers)
London, UK
Owned since 1979 by trusts whose beneficiaries are current and former employees; no external investors
~17,500 members (17,464 at FY2024/25 year end, Arup annual report)
~GBP 2.16bn (year to 31 March 2025)
100 offices; projects in 136 countries (FY2024/25)
CEO Jerome Frost; Non-Executive Chair Hilde Tonne
Los Angeles: yes. San Francisco: yes (first US office, 1985; Oakland too). New York: yes. Madrid: yes (in Spain since 1993). Paris: not confirmed on arup.com - ask.

overview: Arup is an independent consultancy that plans, engineers and advises on buildings, infrastructure, cities and energy. It describes itself as a global consultancy with advisory and technical expertise across more than 150 disciplines, and its stated purpose is to 'guide, plan and design the future of the built environment.' It is famous for structural engineering on landmark buildings, but much of its work today is advisory: climate, resilience, energy, water, transport planning and economics.

Arup has been owned by employee trusts since 1979, so there are no outside shareholders. Staff are called 'members' and share in the firm's profits. In FY2024/25 (year to 31 March 2025) Arup reported about GBP 2.16bn revenue, about 17,500 members and 100 offices, after a restructuring that reduced headcount by 810. In the US it has 13 offices and over 2,000 people; San Francisco, opened in 1985, was the first.

What makes Arup distinctive is that its culture still runs on founder Ove Arup's 1970 'Key Speech', which set out six values including 'social usefulness' and 'Total Architecture' (integrating every design decision through one team). The firm says sustainable development 'lies at the heart' of its approach, and it has taken visible stances such as refusing new hydrocarbon energy commissions since April 2022.
sustainability: Net zero: in 2020 Arup committed to net zero across its operations by 2030 with SBTi-validated targets; its commitments page now frames the goal as becoming a science-based net zero organisation by 2040 (financial year ending March 2040).
Progress: Arup's FY2024/25 global footprint was 109,802 tCO2e, a 39% cut from its FY2018/19 baseline; emissions per member are down 48%.

Fossil fuel stance: at COP26 Arup committed not to pursue work supporting extraction, refining or transport of hydrocarbon fuels; since 1 April 2022 it takes no new such energy commissions (hydrogen manufacture excepted) and says its renewables work has more than doubled.
Whole life carbon: also at COP26, Arup committed to whole life carbon assessments for all its building projects, new build and retrofit, and reported progress in March 2024.

Pledges and networks: Race to Zero, The Climate Pledge, WorldGBC Net Zero Carbon Buildings Commitment, WEF Alliance of CEO Climate Leaders, Business for Nature Call to Action, and the UN Global Compact (signatory since 2010).

Resilience research: with support from the Rockefeller Foundation, Arup developed the City Resilience Framework and City Resilience Index (52 indicators, 156 questions, 12 goals) for cities to self-assess resilience.
Social value: in FY2024/25 members gave 41,305 pro bono community engagement hours and Arup invested GBP 4m in community engagement.

projects.name: Sydney Opera House
projects.why: Arup was appointed engineer in 1957 and solved the roof shells with repeatable, prefabricated geometry; it still works on the building's care 60+ years later.

projects.name: Centre Pompidou
projects.why: Arup engineered the 1977 inside-out building with Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers, a defining example of exposed structure and services.

projects.name: California Academy of Sciences
projects.why: Arup led engineering and sustainability: LEED Platinum, a 2.5-acre living roof, ~34% less energy and ~77% less water.

projects.name: Beijing National Aquatics Centre (Water Cube)
projects.why: A 2008 Olympic venue whose structure is based on Weaire-Phelan foam and wrapped in ETFE pillows to act as an insulated, daylit greenhouse.

projects.name: BIQ House SolarLeaf facade
projects.why: Arup co-developed the first full-scale microalgae bioreactor facade (2013), producing biomass and heat while shading the building.

projects.name: City Resilience Index
projects.why: A self-assessment tool that gives cities a baseline resilience profile across 52 indicators to plan and track improvements.

culture: Six guiding values from Ove Arup's 1970 Key Speech: quality of work, Total Architecture, humane organisation, straight and honourable dealings, social usefulness, and reasonable prosperity of members.
Employee trust ownership: no external shareholders, staff are 'members', and the firm frames this as freedom to choose work that matters.
Strongly multidisciplinary: 150+ disciplines; teams mix engineers, planners, scientists, economists and designers ('Total Architecture').
FY2024/25 people stats: 81% of members said they are proud to work at Arup; the Executive Board was 50/50 gender balanced.

Early careers: Arup hires 'hundreds of graduates globally' each year and offers internships; its early careers page stresses collaboration across disciplines, continuous learning and lasting environmental and social impact.
Mobility: 2.7% of members were on international assignment in FY2024/25, so moving between offices (e.g. US to Madrid) is a known path.
lookFor: Collaboration across backgrounds and disciplines - show you can work with engineers and translate between technical and non-technical people.
Open-mindedness, adaptability and continuous learning (named on Arup's early careers page).
Creative problem solving and a commitment to high-quality work ('quality of work' is a founding value).
Genuine motivation to create lasting environmental and social impact - link your environmental studies work to 'social usefulness'.
Ability to frame sustainability as evidence and analysis (carbon, resilience, data) that clients can act on, since much of Arup's climate work is advisory.

Arup's COP26 commitments: whole life carbon assessments on all building projects and no new hydrocarbon commissions from April 2022.
The California Academy of Sciences in SF: LEED Platinum, 2.5-acre living roof, about 77% less water.
Arup's FY2024/25 carbon footprint was 39% below its 2018/19 baseline, while pursuing a science-based net zero target.

companies.name: Gensler
companies.tagline: The world's largest architecture and design firm, a privately held, employee-owned practice founded in San Francisco.

facts.v: 1965 in San Francisco by Art Gensler, Drue Gensler and James (Jim) Follett
San Francisco, California
Privately held and employee-owned
~6,000 people (gensler.com, 2026)
58 offices in 16 countries (gensler.com, 2026)
~US$1.88bn (2024, reported; often ranked largest architecture firm by revenue)
Co-CEOs Jordan Goldstein and Julia Simet (since Jan 2024); Global Co-Chairs Andy Cohen and Diane Hoskins
"To create a better world through the power of design"
Los Angeles: yes. San Francisco: yes (HQ; also Oakland, San Jose). New York: yes. Paris: yes. Madrid: no (European offices are Berlin, Birmingham, London, Munich, Paris).

overview: Gensler is a global architecture, interior design, planning and consulting firm. It began in 1965 as a one-room San Francisco office focused on corporate interiors and grew into the largest architecture firm in the world by revenue, with about 6,000 people in 58 offices across 16 countries. It works across 33 practice areas, from workplace, aviation and mixed-use to cities, real estate strategy and building conversions.

The firm is organized as one connected global practice rather than a set of separate offices: Art Gensler deliberately built a collaborative 'one-firm firm' culture instead of a star-architect model, reinforced by employee ownership. Since January 2024 it has been led by co-CEOs Jordan Goldstein and Julia Simet, with long-time co-CEOs Andy Cohen and Diane Hoskins as global co-chairs.

What makes Gensler distinctive for sustainability is scale plus data. It says it touches over 1.25 billion square feet of buildings each year, so its 2030 net zero portfolio pledge (GC3), its open-source product sustainability standards and its research institute can shift the whole industry. Its consulting side advises clients on workplace and real estate portfolio strategy, which is where decisions to renovate, consolidate, convert or build get made.
sustainability: Gensler Cities Climate Challenge (GC3): launched in 2019 at the UN Climate Action Summit; the firm pledges to eliminate all net emissions associated with its work by 2030, covering both operational and embodied carbon.
Scale of influence: Gensler says it touches over 1.25 billion square feet of buildings and spaces each year, more than any other design firm.

Progress reporting: an annual report (formerly Impact by Design, now Climate Action Through Design) tracks the portfolio; Gensler estimates a recent portfolio would avoid 8.9 million metric tons CO2e, a 68% cut in operational carbon (self-reported).

Gensler Product Sustainability (GPS) Standards: introduced in 2023 and required on US, Canadian and European projects from January 2024; v2.0 launched in 2025 as an open-source framework with an interactive table for material criteria.

Pledges and partnerships: signed the Paris Pledge for Action at COP21 (2015) and, at COP28 (Dec 2023), agreed with IFC to promote EDGE green building certification and train Gensler design leaders in it.
Gensler Research Institute: six research pillars (Workplace, Cities, Health, Lifestyle, Equity, Resilience), 50+ research grants a year, and studies such as a Global Climate Action survey.
Reuse over new build: Gensler's building conversion tool has analyzed more than 1,300 buildings for office-to-residential and other conversions.
Recognition: ranked #1 on Interior Design's 2026 Sustainability Giants list and repeatedly ENR's #1 Top Green Design Firm.

projects.name: Shanghai Tower
projects.why: Gensler's 632-meter supertall earned LEED Platinum and China Green Building Three Star ratings, with a double-skin facade that buffers heating and cooling loads.

projects.name: SFO Harvey Milk Terminal 1
projects.why: Gensler reports a 79% cut in 50-year total carbon and a 70% cut in energy use intensity under SFO's Triple Zero (carbon, energy, waste) framework.

projects.name: SFO Terminal 2 renovation
projects.why: Reopened in 2011 as the first US airport terminal certified LEED Gold, reusing most of the 1954 structure.

projects.name: The Old Post Office
projects.why: Gensler led the adaptive reuse of a 2.8-million-square-foot historic post office into offices, reopened in 2019 - a model of reusing embodied carbon.

projects.name: 160 Water Street (office-to-residential conversion)
projects.why: Converting a downtown office tower into 588 homes shows how reuse can tackle housing shortages and avoid new construction.

culture: 'One-firm firm': Art Gensler rejected the star-architect model for a team-based 'we, not me' culture and a client-first approach.
Employee-owned and privately held, which the firm links to a shared-ownership identity.
Research-driven: the Gensler Research Institute funds 50+ research grants a year and publishes the Design Forecast and Global Workplace Survey.
Early careers: 3,500+ interns hosted from 60+ schools; a traditional internship in offices and a research-focused Summer Fellowship on the future of cities.
Sustainability mantra 'Every Person, Every Project, Every Place' - climate goals apply across every practice area, not just a specialist team.
Planned leadership succession: co-CEOs Goldstein and Simet took over in January 2024 after nearly 20 years of Cohen and Hoskins.
lookFor: 'Bold and bright' people from a wide range of backgrounds (Gensler's internships page) - environmental studies is a differentiator, not a gap.
Research and analytical skills: surveys, data analysis and clear writing match the Research Institute and Summer Fellowship model.
For consulting/strategy roles, Gensler posts for design analysts in workplace strategy, real estate portfolio strategy, change management and utilization analysis.
Fluency in carbon and materials: operational vs embodied carbon, EPDs and certifications (LEED, EDGE, Fitwel) used under GC3 and GPS.
Ability to tie sustainability to client value - cost, risk, asset performance and people's experience of space.
questions: In enterprise portfolio strategy, how do you weigh embodied carbon when a client is choosing between consolidating, renovating and building new?
How does climate risk or resilience show up in the capital plans you help clients build today?
When a client has surplus office space, how often does the conversion analysis change the portfolio decision?

Where in Gensler would someone with an environmental studies background add the most value early on?
How do early-career people get involved in Gensler Research Institute work?
How has the IFC EDGE partnership changed work in fast-growing markets?
What would you want a new analyst on a portfolio strategy team to master in their first year?
talkingPoints: GC3, launched in 2019, commits Gensler's entire portfolio to net zero by 2030, including embodied carbon - and Gensler touches 1.25 billion sq ft a year.
The GPS Standards became mandatory on US, Canadian and European projects in January 2024 and are open source, so the whole industry can use them.
SFO's Harvey Milk Terminal 1: Gensler reports a 79% cut in 50-year total carbon - a local SF example.
Building reuse: the Old Post Office in Chicago and the 160 Water Street conversion in NYC, plus a conversion tool that has assessed 1,300+ buildings.
At COP28 Gensler partnered with IFC to train its designers in EDGE certification and expand green finance.
The Gensler Research Institute's six pillars include Resilience and Equity, connecting climate to people.

companies.name: Arcadis
companies.tagline: Dutch-founded, Euronext-listed design, engineering and consultancy firm focused on resilience, places and mobility.

facts.v: 1888 in the Netherlands as the Nederlandsche Heidemaatschappij, reclaiming wetlands for farming; Arcadis name from 1997
Amsterdam, Netherlands (US HQ: Highlands Ranch, Colorado)
Publicly listed on Euronext Amsterdam (left NASDAQ in 2007); the Lovinklaan Foundation is its largest shareholder (per 2020 UN-Habitat release)
34,000+ employees ('Arcadians') in 30+ countries (arcadis.com, 2026)
~EUR 4.87bn gross / ~EUR 3.76bn net revenues (2025)
CEO Heather Polinsky (from 1 March 2026, confirmed by shareholders May 2026); succeeded Alan Brookes
Global Business Areas: Resilience, Places, Mobility (Intelligence folded mainly into Mobility from Jan 2026)
Madrid: yes (Torre Rioja). Paris: yes (rue Raymond Losserand). Los Angeles, San Francisco, New York: appear as office locations in Arcadis job postings (250+ offices worldwide).

overview: Arcadis is a global design, engineering and consultancy company that says it 'puts imagination to work to solve critical infrastructure and environmental challenges.' It started in 1888 turning Dutch wetlands into farmland, and water and environment are still at its core. Today it has 34,000+ employees in 30+ countries and reported about EUR 3.8bn net revenues in 2025.

Since 2022 Arcadis has been organized into Global Business Areas. Resilience covers water, environmental restoration, energy transition, climate adaptation and permitting; Places covers buildings, property and investment advisory and technology facilities; Mobility covers transport infrastructure. Its digital 'Intelligence' products are being folded mostly into Mobility from January 2026. It grew through acquisitions such as Malcolm Pirnie (water, 2009), EC Harris (2011), Hyder and Callison (2014) and IBI Group (2022).

Arcadis is in transition: Heather Polinsky, who previously ran the Resilience business (its most profitable area), became CEO in March 2026 after a mixed 2025 that included cutting about 1,100 roles. She plans to present a new three-year strategy at a Capital Markets Day in November 2026, so this is a good moment to ask where the firm is heading.
sustainability: Net zero 2035: Arcadis commits to net zero greenhouse gas emissions across its value chain by 2035, with SBTi-approved targets.
Interim targets: cut absolute scope 1 and 2 emissions 70% by 2026 and scope 3 emissions 45% by 2029 (both vs 2019); electric company fleet by 2030; 100% renewable electricity for offices.
Nature: aims to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030, with no net biodiversity loss at its sites and a 10% net biodiversity gain at sites with significant green space by 2030.

Resilience business: energy transition, climate adaptation, water optimization, environmental restoration and permitting; its Climate Risk Nexus tool with Jupiter Intelligence grew from 2 pilots in 2024 to 20 projects in 2025.
Sustainable Cities Index: Arcadis' research ranking of 100 cities on Planet, People and Profit; the 2024 edition (6th since 2015) added a Progress pillar and ranked Amsterdam first.
Shelter program: a pro bono partnership with UN-Habitat since 2010 supporting sustainable urban planning, water, climate adaptation and disaster recovery (120+ missions by 2020).
Disclosure: publishes a Climate Transition Plan (2024), annual integrated reports and CDP climate responses; Sustainalytics rates it in the top 2% of its industry for ESG performance.

culture: Four operating principles: 'People first, always', 'Turn intent into achievement', 'Build unwavering trust' and 'Impact beyond business'.
Employees call themselves 'Arcadians'; the careers site highlights flexibility, remote options and a globally connected community.
North America hires 300+ new graduates and 100+ interns in a typical year; internships last 10-12 weeks and most are hired in May and June.
Development support includes mentoring, help with professional certifications and conference presentations, and a 'Your Voice' feedback survey.
Recognized as a leading ambassador in the Workplace Pride Global Benchmark for LGBTIQ+ inclusion and among Fast Company's Most Innovative Companies 2024.
A period of change: new CEO in 2026, a simplification push and a new strategy due in November 2026.

Arcadis is widening its graduate pipeline to urban planning and digital roles.
A passion for improving quality of life and making a positive impact (the firm's purpose is improving quality of life).
Fresh thinking and new perspectives - people who will challenge the status quo.
Practical field and data skills (GIS, sampling, regulatory knowledge) that support remediation, water and climate adaptation projects.

cards.q: In what year was Arcadis founded?
cards.explain: Arcadis traces its roots to 1888 in the Netherlands, giving it 135+ years of history.

cards.q: What was Arcadis' original purpose?
cards.a: Turning unusable Dutch wetlands into farmland
cards.explain: It began as a land reclamation business converting wetlands into productive farms.

cards.q: What was Arcadis' original name?
cards.explain: The Heidemaatschappij split in 1974; the Heidemij business later became Arcadis.

cards.q: When was the Arcadis name introduced?
cards.explain: The name arrived in 1997; the brand was rolled out globally in 2015 as legacy brands were phased out.

cards.q: Where is Arcadis headquartered?
cards.explain: Arcadis N.V. is based in Amsterdam; its US headquarters is in Highlands Ranch, Colorado.

cards.q: Where are Arcadis shares listed?
cards.explain: Arcadis voluntarily delisted from NASDAQ in 2007 and trades on Euronext.

cards.q: Which of these is an Arcadis operating principle?
cards.explain: The four principles are People first always, Turn intent into achievement, Build unwavering trust, Impact beyond business.

cards.q: Which 2009 acquisition gave Arcadis a leading global position in water?
cards.explain: Malcolm Pirnie was a US water specialist; other deals included EC Harris (2011) and Hyder (2014).

cards.q: Which Canadian firm did Arcadis acquire in 2022?
cards.explain: Arcadis bought IBI Group, DPS Group and Giftge Consulting in 2022.

cards.q: About how many employees does Arcadis have?
cards.explain: Arcadis' own site cites 34,000+ Arcadians in 30+ countries.

cards.q: What do Arcadis employees call themselves?
cards.explain: The company profile describes its people as 34,000+ Arcadians.

cards.q: What were Arcadis' net revenues in 2025?
cards.explain: Net revenues were EUR 3.76bn, down 0.5% organically; gross revenues were about EUR 4.87bn.

cards.q: Who became Arcadis CEO on 1 March 2026?
cards.explain: She succeeded Alan Brookes; shareholders confirmed her appointment on 20 May 2026.

cards.q: Which business did Heather Polinsky lead before becoming CEO?
cards.explain: Arcadis describes Resilience as its most profitable Global Business Area.

cards.q: What are Arcadis' main Global Business Areas in 2026?
cards.explain: Intelligence products are being integrated into these areas, mostly Mobility, from January 2026.

cards.q: By what year does Arcadis aim for net zero across its value chain?
cards.explain: The target covers scopes 1, 2 and 3 and is approved by the Science Based Targets initiative.

cards.q: What is Arcadis' interim target for scope 1 and 2 emissions?
cards.explain: Scope 3 has a separate target of a 45% cut by 2029 from the same 2019 baseline.

cards.q: What biodiversity gain does Arcadis target at sites with significant green space?
cards.explain: It also aims for no net biodiversity loss at all sites and to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030.

cards.q: Which UN agency partners with Arcadis on the Shelter program?
cards.explain: Since 2010 Arcadis has provided pro bono expertise on UN-Habitat projects, from planning to disaster recovery.

cards.q: What does Arcadis' Sustainable Cities Index measure?
cards.explain: It ranks cities on Planet, People and Profit; the 2024 edition added a Progress pillar.

cards.q: Which city ranked first in the 2024 Sustainable Cities Index?
cards.explain: Amsterdam topped the 2024 index, with Copenhagen third and Munich fifth.

cards.q: Which company co-developed Arcadis' Climate Risk Nexus tool?
cards.explain: The climate risk analytics tool grew from 2 pilots in 2024 to 20 active projects in 2025.

cards.q: What did Arcadis' Lower Manhattan resilience master plan propose?
cards.a: Extending the shoreline up to 500 feet and raising it 20+ feet
cards.explain: The plan for the Financial District and Seaport aims to protect against storm surge and sea level rise.
wrong: A movable surge barrier across New York Harbor
Relocating residents away from the waterfront

cards.q: What is the Marker Wadden project Arcadis worked on?
cards.a: Islands built to restore Lake Markermeer's ecosystem
cards.explain: Arcadis helped design the islands and managed licensing for this large ecosystem restoration in the Netherlands.
wrong: A North Sea storm surge barrier

cards.q: What did Arcadis propose for flood-prone Buzi District, Mozambique?
cards.a: A network of raised refuge platforms
cards.explain: Working with UN-Habitat, it proposed elevated sites like schools that stay dry so life continues during floods.
